client: Lately, I've been feeling so stressed about money since my partner got laid off. I'm working overtime just to cover everything, but we keep fighting about spending habits and it's making me resentful. I don't know if talking about it will help when the real problem is our bank account.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load right now, both financially and emotionally. When you mention feeling resentful, I wonder if you're also feeling unheard in these money discussions—would you say that's accurate?  

What thoughts come up for you when these fights about spending happen?

client:
Yeah, that's definitely part of it. When we argue about money, I keep thinking "here we go again" and just shut down because it feels like my concerns never actually get addressed. I try to explain why certain expenses stress me out, but it always turns into me being the "uptight" one while they keep spending.  

The worst part is I do feel guilty for resenting them, because I know they're not trying to be irresponsible on purpose. But then the cycle just repeats and I end up feeling both angry and ashamed.
therapist:
I hear how stuck you feel in this painful cycle—where your very real concerns get dismissed, leaving you both frustrated and guilty. That "here we go again" thought seems to reinforce the shutdown, almost like a script you expect to play out.  

Could we explore what happens *before* that thought arises? For example, what’s the first physical or emotional cue that tells you the conversation is heading toward that familiar argument?

client:
I guess the first cue is this tightness in my chest when I start explaining how I feel. It's like my body already knows they're going to brush me off before they even respond. Then I get this hot, prickly feeling behind my eyes like I'm about to cry from frustration. 

But I don't know if noticing these physical things will actually help - it's not like my body reacting differently will make other people listen to me any better.
therapist:
It makes sense that your body reacts so strongly—it’s carrying the weight of these repeated disappointments. That tightness and prickling might actually be important signals, not just reactions.  

What if we tried shifting focus for a moment? When you notice those physical cues, what’s one small way you could respond to *yourself* with kindness in that moment, regardless of how the conversation goes?

client: I get what you're saying about being kind to myself, but honestly when I feel that tightness in my chest, my first instinct is to beat myself up for reacting that way again. It's like a cycle - I feel anxious, then I get mad at myself for being anxious. The idea of self-kindness feels... foreign, I guess? Like I don't really deserve it when I'm in that state.
therapist:
It sounds like self-criticism has become almost automatic for you in those moments—like a reflex that kicks in before kindness even has a chance. That "foreign" feeling makes so much sense when you’ve been stuck in this cycle for so long.  

I wonder: if you *did* deserve kindness in those moments (and you do), what might that look or sound like to you? Even something as small as a single reassuring phrase?

client:
I don't know... the idea of being kind to myself in those moments just feels fake, like I'd be lying to myself. When I mess up at work or say something awkward, the voice in my head says "of course you screwed up, you always do" and that feels more honest than trying to force some positive mantra. 

It's not that I don't believe you about deserving kindness, it's just that the critical voice has been with me for so long that anything else feels unnatural. Like putting on clothes that don't fit right.
therapist:
That critical voice has been your constant companion for so long that challenging it feels like betraying an old, if painful, truth. It makes perfect sense that forced positivity would ring hollow—we’re not aiming for that.  

What if we started smaller? Instead of trying to *replace* that critical voice right away, could we simply *notice* it with curiosity? Like observing, "Ah, there’s that familiar voice again"—without either believing it or fighting it? How does that idea sit with you?

client: That idea sounds... okay, I guess. But honestly, it feels a little abstract. How do I just "notice" it without getting sucked into believing it? Every time I hear that voice, it feels so real, like it’s telling me the truth about myself. It’s hard to just observe it without reacting. I don’t know if I can separate myself from it that easily.
therapist:
It makes total sense that this feels abstract—and that the voice feels so convincing in the moment. That "realness" is exactly what makes it so powerful. Let’s try grounding it in something concrete: next time the critical voice shows up, could you pause and ask yourself, *"Would I say this to a close friend feeling the same way?"* Not to force kindness, just to highlight the mismatch. How does that land for you?  

(Their slightly negative valence and mild arousal suggest they're skeptical but not overwhelmed—good space for a practical, slightly challenging question.)

client: I get the idea behind treating myself like a friend, but it feels forced. When I'm in that critical headspace, it's like I *know* I wouldn't say this to someone else, but it doesn't stop me from believing it about myself. The logic just doesn't sink in when I'm spiraling.
therapist:
It sounds like you’re caught in a tricky gap—where you can intellectually recognize the unfairness of the critical voice, but emotionally, it still feels true. That disconnect can be so frustrating to navigate.  

When you’re spiraling, what’s one small action (even just taking a deep breath or stepping outside for a moment) that might create just enough space to pause the spiral, even if it doesn’t stop the thoughts completely?

client: I get what you're saying about creating space, but when I'm spiraling, it feels like everything is happening too fast for me to even think about pausing. The critical voice feels so loud and overwhelming that even taking a deep breath seems impossible in the moment. I guess I’m skeptical that something so small could make a difference when I’m already so deep in it.
therapist:
I hear how all-consuming that spiral feels—like the critical voice leaves no room for even the smallest pause. When everything feels so immediate and loud, it makes perfect sense that even a deep breath feels out of reach.  

What if we shifted focus to *before* the spiral starts? Are there any early physical signs—like tension in your shoulders or quickened breathing—that might signal the spiral is coming, when a small pause *might* still feel possible?

client:
I never really thought about catching it before it starts... that feels overwhelming. When I try to notice my body, it just makes me more anxious about what's coming. Like now I'm tensing up just thinking about it.  

But I guess sometimes my hands do get shaky first, or my stomach knots up before the thoughts really take over. It's just hard to pay attention to those signs when everything feels so urgent.
therapist:
It sounds like tuning into your body brings up its own layer of anxiety—almost like watching storm clouds roll in and feeling powerless to stop them. Those early signs (the shaky hands, the knotted stomach) are important clues, but I hear how scary it feels to notice them.  

What if we tried something different: next time you feel those physical cues, could you simply name them quietly—*"shaky hands" or "tight stomach"*—without judging or trying to change them? Just noticing, like observing weather passing through. How does that approach sit with you?

client:
I get what you're saying, but naming the feelings out loud makes me feel even more aware of them, and that just ramps up my anxiety. It's like when you try not to think about a pink elephant—suddenly it's all you can focus on.  

I worry that if I say "shaky hands," I'll just start hyper-fixating on how bad it feels instead of it actually helping. Does that make sense? I don't want to make it worse.
therapist:
That makes complete sense—it’s like the act of naming them turns up the volume instead of lowering it. Hyper-fixating can absolutely make the physical sensations feel even bigger, and I appreciate you naming that worry so clearly.  

What if we shifted focus to something outside your body for a moment? When you notice those shaky hands, could you try quietly naming *one thing you see* in the room instead—just to give your mind a tiny anchor outside of the spiral? Not to stop the feelings, just to create a sliver of space alongside them. How does that idea land?
